objectives: Explain how the equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity are determined.
Explain why a surplus (excess supply) or a shortage (excess demand) pushes the price toward equilibrium.
Use a four-step analysis to find the new equilibrium when demand or supply changes, and evaluate the effects of price ceilings and price floors.

concepts.definition: The situation in which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. The price at that point is the equilibrium price, and the quantity is the equilibrium quantity.

If the price is above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and there is a surplus. If the price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and there is a shortage. Do not confuse this surplus with consumer surplus and producer surplus, which are different ideas (the gains buyers and sellers get from trade) used in later lessons.

concepts.term: Four-step analysis of a change in equilibrium
concepts.definition: (1) Draw the original market. (2) Decide whether demand or supply changed. (3) Decide which direction the curve shifts. (4) Compare the new equilibrium with the original one.

A price ceiling sets the highest price that sellers may legally charge; a price floor sets the lowest price that buyers may legally pay. A ceiling set below equilibrium creates a shortage, and a floor set above equilibrium creates a surplus.

beginner.summary: The market price is the price where the amount people want to buy matches the amount sellers want to sell. When goods are left over, the price falls; when there is not enough, the price rises, until the market finds that price.

sections.heading: Finding the price that fits
paragraphs: Imagine you are selling fresh donuts at a school festival. If you charge too much, few customers come. If you charge too little, a long line forms. At the price where the amount people want to buy equals the amount you want to sell, nothing is left over and no one goes without. This price is called the equilibrium price.

sections.heading: Leftovers push prices down; shortfalls push them up
paragraphs: If lots of donuts are left over, the seller will cut the price to sell them. If the donuts sell out fast and customers are still lining up, the seller can raise the price and still sell them all. In this way, leftovers (a surplus) and shortfalls (a shortage) push the price toward equilibrium.

sections.heading: When conditions change, the market price changes
paragraphs: On a cold day, more people want a warm donut (an increase in demand), so the price rises and more donuts are sold. If flour gets more expensive (a decrease in supply), the price rises and fewer donuts are sold. First figure out what changed, then work out step by step how the price and quantity change.

sections.heading: What if the government sets the price?
paragraphs: Suppose the government says, "No one may charge more than 50 cents for a donut," setting a maximum price below the market price. More people want to buy, but fewer sellers want to bake, so there are not enough donuts. If the government instead sets a minimum price above the market price, unsold goods pile up. Even well-meaning policies can have side effects like these, so we need to weigh them.

intermediate.summary: Equilibrium is where the demand and supply curves intersect. At any other price, a surplus or shortage puts pressure on the price to adjust, and a four-step analysis finds the new equilibrium after demand or supply shifts.

sections.heading: Equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity
paragraphs: Where the demand curve and the supply curve cross, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. The price and quantity at that point are the equilibrium price (P*) and the equilibrium quantity (Q*). At equilibrium, everyone who wants to buy at that price can buy, and everyone who wants to sell at that price can sell.

sections.heading: Surpluses, shortages, and price adjustment
paragraphs: If P > P*, quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, creating a surplus (excess supply), and sellers lower their prices. If P < P*, quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied, creating a shortage (excess demand); buyers accept higher prices and sellers raise them. This pressure continues until the price reaches equilibrium.

sections.heading: The four-step analysis
paragraphs: (1) Draw the original market → (2) decide whether the event changes demand or supply → (3) decide whether the curve shifts right (an increase) or left (a decrease) → (4) compare the new intersection with the original one.

Summary: demand increases → price↑, quantity↑ / demand decreases → price↓, quantity↓ / supply increases → price↓, quantity↑ / supply decreases → price↑, quantity↓. When demand and supply change at the same time, the direction of one of the two (price or quantity) depends on the sizes of the two shifts. (See Example 4.)

sections.heading: Price ceilings and price floors
paragraphs: A price ceiling below equilibrium raises quantity demanded and lowers quantity supplied, creating a shortage. A shortage can lead to other ways of rationing the good, such as waiting in line, lower quality, or black markets.
A price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus. When the government buys up the extra output, as with farm price supports, the cost falls on taxpayers and consumers.

advanced.summary: In a linear model, equilibrium is the solution of a system of equations, P* = (a − c)/(b + d). Comparative statics shows how parameter changes affect the outcome, and under price controls you can calculate the size of a shortage or surplus.

sections.heading: Calculating equilibrium
paragraphs: With Qd = a − bP and Qs = c + dP, the equilibrium condition Qd = Qs gives a − bP = c + dP, so P* = (a − c)/(b + d) and Q* = a − bP*. A positive equilibrium requires a > c and Q* > 0.

sections.heading: Disequilibrium and adjustment
paragraphs: At any price P, excess demand is ED(P) = Qd − Qs = (a − c) − (b + d)P. If ED > 0 there is a shortage, and if ED < 0 there is a surplus. ED falls as P rises and equals 0 at P*. If we assume the price moves in the direction of the sign of excess demand, the price converges to P*.

sections.heading: Comparative statics
paragraphs: Since ∂P*/∂a = 1/(b + d) > 0, an increase in demand (higher a) raises the equilibrium price. Since ∂P*/∂c = −1/(b + d) < 0, an increase in supply (higher c) lowers the equilibrium price. The larger b and d are (the more price-sensitive buyers and sellers are, measured in units per dollar, not as an elasticity), the smaller the price change caused by the same shock.
These results are the four-step analysis written in equations. The equations let you compare not only the direction of a change but also its size.

sections.heading: Quantitative analysis of price controls
paragraphs: With a price ceiling P̄ < P*, the quantity actually traded falls to the quantity supplied, Qs(P̄), and the shortage is Qd(P̄) − Qs(P̄). Because fewer units are traded than at equilibrium, some gains from trade are lost to society as a whole; this loss is called deadweight loss. In a linear model, it is the area of the triangle between the equilibrium quantity and the quantity actually traded, bounded by the demand curve (the price consumers are willing to pay) and the supply curve (the minimum price producers must receive). This triangle assumes that the units that are traded go to the buyers who value them most and that rationing itself costs nothing. If waiting in line, searching, or black markets use up time and resources, the loss is larger. (See Example 5.)

When evaluating a policy, ask together: Who gains and who loses? By how much? Is there another tool that could reach the same goal (for example, food access for low-income households) with fewer side effects?

worked_examples.title: Finding the equilibrium price from a table
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: When a sandwich costs $2, quantity demanded is 60 and quantity supplied is 20. At $3, quantity demanded is 40 and quantity supplied is 40. At $4, quantity demanded is 20 and quantity supplied is 60. What is the equilibrium price?
steps: Look for the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
At $2 there is a shortage of 40 sandwiches, and at $4 there is a surplus of 40 sandwiches.
worked_examples.answer: The equilibrium price is $3, and the equilibrium quantity is 40 sandwiches.

worked_examples.title: Four-step analysis: fertilizer prices rise
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: The price of fertilizer has risen sharply. How do the equilibrium price and quantity in the rice market change?
steps: (1) Draw demand, supply, and the equilibrium in the original rice market.
(2) Fertilizer is a production cost, so supply changes.
(3) Higher costs → farmers produce less at every price → the supply curve shifts left.
(4) The new intersection is up and to the left of the original: price↑, quantity↓.
worked_examples.answer: The equilibrium price rises and the equilibrium quantity falls.

worked_examples.title: Equilibrium and the shortage under a price ceiling
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: In a flour market, Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 10 + P. (1) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (2) If the government sets a price ceiling of 24, how large is the shortage?
steps: Shortage = 52 − 34 = 18. The quantity actually traded is the quantity supplied, 34, which is 6 less than at equilibrium.

worked_examples.title: When demand and supply change together
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: During a summer festival, more people want milkshakes (an increase in demand). At the same time, the price of milk rises, so shops make fewer milkshakes (a decrease in supply). What can you say for sure about the equilibrium price and quantity of milkshakes?
steps: The increase in demand alone: price↑, quantity↑.
The decrease in supply alone: price↑, quantity↓.
Both changes push the price up, so the price definitely rises.
One change raises quantity and the other lowers it, so the effect on quantity depends on whether demand rose by more or supply fell by more.
worked_examples.answer: The equilibrium price rises. The equilibrium quantity could rise or fall, depending on the sizes of the two shifts.

worked_examples.title: Calculating the deadweight loss of a price ceiling
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: A price ceiling of 24 is placed on the flour market from Example 3 (Qd = 100 − 2P, Qs = 10 + P, equilibrium P* = 30, Q* = 40). How large are the gains from trade lost because fewer units are traded (the deadweight loss)?
steps: At the ceiling of 24, the quantity actually traded is the quantity supplied, Qs = 10 + 24 = 34 (6 less than the equilibrium quantity of 40).
The price consumers are willing to pay for the 34th unit: solve the demand function for P, P = (100 − Q)/2 → (100 − 34)/2 = 33.
The minimum price needed to produce the 34th unit: solve the supply function for P, P = Q − 10 → 34 − 10 = 24.
The deadweight loss is the area of the triangle between quantities 34 and 40 = ½ × (40 − 34) × (33 − 24) = ½ × 6 × 9 = 27.
worked_examples.answer: The deadweight loss is 27 (price units × quantity units). This assumes the 34 units go to the buyers who value them most and that rationing itself costs nothing; queuing, search, or black markets would make the loss larger.

graphs.title: Equilibrium and a price ceiling
graphs.caption: Hypothetical example. Equilibrium is at P = 30, Q = 40. At a price ceiling of 24, quantity demanded is 52 and quantity supplied is 34, a shortage of 18.

real_world_examples.title: Rent control and housing shortages
paragraphs: If rents are held below the market level, more people look for apartments while fewer landlords offer them, which can cause a shortage. Critics also point out that landlords may spend less on repairs and upkeep, so housing quality can decline.

real_world_examples.title: Farm price supports and surpluses
paragraphs: Many high-income countries have supported farm prices above equilibrium to protect farmers' incomes. Higher prices increase production and reduce consumption, creating a surplus, and the cost of the government buying that surplus is borne by taxpayers and consumers.

sdg_case.title: When food prices spike: a price ceiling or direct support?
paragraphs: SDG 2 aims for stable access to food for everyone, and SDG 12 aims for sustainable consumption and production. Hypothetical situation: Rising world grain prices have pushed up the prices of bread and noodles sharply, putting pressure on low-income households.
There are several tools for reaching the same goal (food access for vulnerable households), and each has different side effects on the market. Use the demand and supply model to compare them.

options.name: Put a price ceiling on bread and noodles
benefits: Every consumer can buy at a lower price right away.
costs: If the ceiling is below the equilibrium price, quantity supplied falls while quantity demanded rises, which can cause shortages, lines, and lower quality.
Better-off households get the same benefit.
assumptions: Side effects stay small only if the ceiling is close to the equilibrium price; the further below equilibrium it is set, the larger the shortage.

options.name: Give food vouchers or cash to low-income households
benefits: Help can be focused on the households that need it.
Prices are not capped, so sellers have no reason to cut the quantity they supply.
costs: It costs public money, plus administrative costs to select recipients and make payments.
If supply does not increase, the extra demand may push prices up a bit more.
assumptions: The government can identify eligible households accurately and deliver support quickly.

options.name: Support the supply side (more imports, help with production costs)
benefits: Shifts the supply curve to the right, which can bring the price itself down.
costs: It takes time for the effects to show up.
Subsidies cost public money and can encourage overproduction or waste (a tension with SDG 12).
assumptions: Import sources are available, and cost support actually leads to more production.

discussion: Which tool fits best in the short run (a few weeks), and which in the long run (several years)? Write down your reasoning and the assumptions behind it.

key_takeaways: Equilibrium is the point where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; surpluses and shortages push the price toward equilibrium.
When demand or supply changes, use the four-step analysis to find how the equilibrium price and quantity change.
Price ceilings and floors can create shortages and surpluses their designers did not intend, so compare their costs and benefits with other tools that pursue the same goal.
